title: Green Chemistry and the Future of Materials

cards.h: Making things without making a mess
cards.b: Chemistry gave us medicines, fertiliser and plastics, but also pollution. Green chemistry asks a design question: can we make what we need while creating less waste and less hazard from the start? It prevents pollution rather than cleaning it later.

Paul Anastas and John Warner (1998) listed 12 principles. Key ones:

  • Prevent waste rather than treat it.
  • Maximise atom economy.
  • Use safer chemicals and solvents.
  • Design for energy efficiency.
  • Use renewable feedstocks and catalysts.
  • Design products that degrade after use.

Atom economy = (mass of desired product / total mass of reactants) x 100. A reaction can have a high yield yet waste atoms in by-products.

Addition reactions can reach 100 percent: C2H4 + H2 → C2H6 uses every atom.

The E-factor (Roger Sheldon) is kg of waste per kg of product. Oil refining is under 0.1, bulk chemicals 1 to 5, and pharmaceuticals can be 25 to over 100.

Greener solvents: water, supercritical CO2, ionic liquids, or no solvent at all. Catalysts cut energy and waste. Enzymes make drugs at room temperature in water.

Solar cells, wind, and batteries need new materials. Green hydrogen by electrolysis of water with renewable power, 2H2O → 2H2 + O2, offers a fuel and industrial feedstock without CO2. Green ammonia and green steel (reducing iron ore with hydrogen instead of coke) could cut industry's emissions.

• Graphene: one-atom-thick carbon, strong and conducting; Geim and Novoselov isolated it in 2004 (Nobel 2010).
  • Perovskite solar cells: cheap, efficient light absorbers.
  • Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs): sponge-like crystals to capture CO2 or water from air; the 2025 Chemistry Nobel recognised their development.
  • Biodegradable plastics and recycling chemistry.
  • Solid-state and sodium-ion batteries.

Making quicklime: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2. Masses: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56, CO2 = 44. Atom economy of CaO = 56 / 100 x 100 = 56 percent.

E-factor: making 1 kg of drug creates 50 kg waste, so E-factor = 50. Redesigning to 20 kg waste cuts it to 20.

C2H4 + H2 → C2H6: 28 + 2 = 30 in, 30 out: atom economy 100 percent.

• Green chemistry is not recycling alone. It starts at design.
  • High yield does not mean low waste.
  • 'Natural' solvents are not always greener if they need much energy to produce.
  • Green hydrogen only counts as green if the electricity is renewable.

C.N.R. Rao is a leading Indian solid-state and materials chemist, known for work on oxides, nanomaterials and graphene. He received the Bharat Ratna in 2013. India co-founded the International Solar Alliance (2015) and has set big renewable targets, while the National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023) seeks green hydrogen and ammonia at scale. Indian industry and IITs work on greener catalysts and bio-based chemicals.

• Green chemistry prevents waste: 12 principles (Anastas and Warner, 1998).
  • Atom economy = desired product mass / reactant mass x 100; E-factor = waste per product.
  • Future materials: graphene, perovskites, MOFs, green hydrogen.

Think about it

1. Why can a reaction with 95 percent yield still be wasteful?

2. What would you redesign in a product you use daily to make it greener?
